section.title: Hagar and Sarah
section.sectionRationale: Paul closes his doctrinal argument with an illustration drawn from Abraham's two sons. Hagar the slave woman and Sarah the free woman stand for two covenants: one bearing children into slavery, tied to the present Jerusalem, and one that is free, the Jerusalem above, our mother. As Isaac was a child of promise born by the Spirit, so are believers, and Scripture says to expel the slave woman, for believers are children of the free.
section.thesis: The story of Hagar and Sarah pictures two covenants, one of slavery under law and one of freedom by promise; believers, like Isaac, are children of promise born according to the Spirit, and belong to the free woman and the heavenly Jerusalem, so they must not submit to the slavery of the law.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the two sons of Abraham, one by the slave woman and one by the free; the two covenants they represent, Sinai and slavery versus the Jerusalem above and freedom; and the conclusion, believers are children of promise and of the free woman, not the slave.

units.label: Abraham's two sons
units.note: one by the slave woman, one by the free

verses.text: Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not understand what the law says?
For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman.
His son by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but his son by the free woman was born through the {{epaggelia|promise}}.

units.label: Two covenants
units.note: Sinai and slavery, the Jerusalem above and freedom

verses.text: These things serve as {{allegoreo|illustrations}}, for the women represent two covenants. One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery: This is Hagar.
Now Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children.
But the Jerusalem above is {{eleuthera|free}}, and she is our mother.

For it is written: “Rejoice, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth and cry aloud, you who have never travailed; because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.”

units.label: Children of the free woman
units.note: born by the Spirit, heirs of freedom

verses.text: Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise.
At that time, however, the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit. It is the same now.
But what does the Scripture say? “Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman's son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman's son.”
Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman.

epaggelia.gloss: A promise, a pledge freely given. Isaac was born through the promise, not by human contrivance like Ishmael, who was born according to the flesh. The word marks the whole way of grace: God pledges, and He performs, so that the child of promise owes his existence to God's word and power, not to human effort. Believers are children of promise in the same way.

allegoreo.gloss: To speak allegorically, to use a historical account as an illustration of a deeper truth. Paul is not denying that Hagar and Sarah were real people in real history; he draws out the pattern God built into the story, so that the two women picture two covenants. The account teaches by correspondence, slavery and freedom, flesh and promise.

eleuthera.gloss: Free, the free woman, contrasted with the slave. Sarah is the free woman, and the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of all who belong to Christ. Freedom is the birthright of the children of promise, over against the slavery of those who seek acceptance by the law. It is the same freedom Paul will urge them to stand firm in.

basic.context: Paul makes his final argument to those who want to be under the law, using a story from their own Scriptures. Abraham had two sons: Ishmael, born the ordinary way to Hagar the slave, and Isaac, born by God's promise to Sarah the free woman. Paul says these two women picture two covenants, slavery under law and freedom by promise. Believers are like Isaac, children of promise, so they belong to freedom.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul reads the Old Testament story as a God given picture. He is not making up meaning but drawing out the pattern of slavery and freedom, flesh and promise, that the account contains. Read it as Paul teaching the Galatians to see themselves in Isaac and to refuse the slavery the story warns against.
basic.originalLanguages: Isaac was born through the epaggelia, the promise, not by human effort. Paul calls the story an allegoreo, an illustration that pictures two covenants. Sarah is the eleuthera, the free woman, and the Jerusalem above is free, the mother of all believers.
basic.typology: Isaac, the child of promise born by God's power, is the pattern of every believer born by the Spirit. Sarah and the heavenly Jerusalem picture the covenant of grace. The persecution of Isaac by Ishmael foreshadows the way children of the flesh oppose children of the Spirit, then and now.
basic.christ: The freedom Paul celebrates is the freedom Christ secured. The Jerusalem above, the city of the free, is the community gathered around the risen Christ. Believers are children of promise only because they belong to Christ, the true seed, in whom the promise to Abraham comes true.
basic.god: God is the promise keeper who gave Isaac by His own power and gives new birth by His Spirit. He is the God of the heavenly Jerusalem, gathering a free people. He fulfills the ancient words of Isaiah about the barren woman rejoicing, bringing many children to the once desolate by grace.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 21 tells of Isaac, Ishmael, and the command to send away the slave woman. Isaiah 54 is the song of the barren woman rejoicing that Paul quotes. Hebrews 12 speaks of the heavenly Jerusalem believers have come to.
basic.oneStory: The story of Abraham's household becomes a picture of the whole Bible: slavery under law versus freedom by promise. Believers are children of promise, born by the Spirit, citizens of the Jerusalem above. The gospel gathers a free family, fulfilling Isaiah's vision of the barren woman with countless children.

context.literary:
Galatians 4:21-31 is the last argument of the letter's doctrinal half, and Paul builds it as a trap sprung from the opponents' own library. He has just pleaded with the Galatians in personal terms, 4:12-20, and now he returns to proof, but this time from the Torah itself. The opening question is pointed. Those who want to be under the law are asked whether they have really listened to the law, and the word Paul uses is the ordinary word for hearing. The book they claim to obey, Genesis, has a story in it they have not yet heard.

The passage runs in a tidy sequence. Verses 22 and 23 state the facts of Abraham's household. Verses 24 to 27 draw two columns of correspondence, covenant against covenant, mountain against city, mother against mother, and then support the second column with a quotation from Isaiah 54:1. Verses 28 to 31 apply the whole to the readers, first by naming them Isaac's kin, then by recalling the quarrel in Abraham's house, and finally by quoting Sarah's demand from Genesis 21:10 as though it were a verdict from the court of Scripture.

The form is a list of paired terms, a device ancient teachers used to lay out a chain of associations. Paul stands the pairs in two ranks: Hagar, Ishmael, flesh, Sinai, the present Jerusalem, slavery on one side; Sarah, Isaac, promise, Spirit, the Jerusalem above, freedom on the other. Nothing in the passage is a loose illustration. Every element is placed to push toward the last line, verse 31, and, with it, the opening of chapter 5, where the same ideas become a command.
context.historical:
The Galatian churches were mostly Gentile, and the visitors who followed Paul told them that to belong fully to Abraham's family they must be circumcised and keep the Mosaic law. That teaching had a strong case on paper. God had commanded circumcision of Abraham and every male in his household, Genesis 17:9-14, and Abraham was the father of all who were to be blessed. The agitators could say that Paul had shown Gentiles only half of the way in.

They may also have read the Genesis story with Sarah and Hagar in a way that favoured themselves, treating Isaac's line as the Jewish people and Ishmael's as the outsiders. Paul's reply is bold because he flips that map. In Genesis 16 it was Sarai who devised the plan to build a family through her Egyptian servant, and Abram listened to her voice, Genesis 16:2. Ishmael was born of a human scheme, however sincere. Isaac was born when Abraham and Sarah were beyond hope, Genesis 17:17 and 21:1-2.

The geography matters. Paul says Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia, verse 25. Arabia lay to the south and east of Judea. Paul himself had spent time in Arabia after his conversion, Galatians 1:17. The present Jerusalem, in verse 25, was the centre of the temple and the sort of religion that expected Gentiles to take on Jewish identity. Sinai gave the law, and the Jerusalem of Paul's day was where people were trying to keep it as a boundary marker. The Jerusalem above is a different citizenship altogether.
context.canonical:
Paul draws on two pillars of the Old Testament. The first is Genesis 16 to 21, where the line of promise is sorted out step by step. God had promised Abraham a son by Sarah, Genesis 17:19, and said He would also bless Ishmael, Genesis 17:20, but the covenant would run through Isaac, Genesis 17:21. Paul's reading therefore follows the narrative. Romans 9:6-9 takes the same story from a different angle: not all who descend from Abraham are his children, because 'through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.'

The second pillar is Isaiah 54:1. Isaiah spoke to an exiled people who felt barren, with Jerusalem in ruins. The prophet promised that the desolate woman would have more children than the married one. Isaiah himself had already tied Sarah to that hope, Isaiah 51:2-3, saying God had called Abraham when he was one and made him many, and would make Zion's wilderness like Eden. Paul hears Isaiah's promise reaching its goal in Gentile conversion, so that the barren woman is joined by children from all nations.

The heavenly Jerusalem is not Paul's private invention. Hebrews 12:22 says believers have come to Mount Zion, 'the heavenly Jerusalem,' Revelation 21:2 sees the new Jerusalem coming down out of heaven, and Philippians 3:20 says that our citizenship is in heaven. The Old Testament itself already pictures Zion as a mother of her people, as in Psalm 87 and Isaiah 66:7-13. Paul brings these strands together to say that the city on high belongs to those who believe, and that Sinai is a stage, not the destination, as Galatians 3:19-25 has already argued.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted the Galatians to hear their own Scriptures in the order God had given them. His opponents had presented the law as the way to full membership in Abraham's family. Paul answers that the family was always defined by promise, and he proves it from the very chapter where the family is first sorted into sons of the promise and sons of ordinary effort. His aim is not to teach a theory of allegory but to expose the direction in which the law-keeping movement was leading them.

He also wanted them to feel the stakes. To go back under the law as a means of belonging was not a neutral religious upgrade; it meant choosing the line of Hagar, and the story had ended with Hagar's son sent away. That is why he quotes Genesis 21:10 at the close. The picture is frightening on purpose. At the same time Paul does not leave them with a threat. He ends with an identity: 'we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman,' verse 31. The point of the passage is that they already are free, and Paul expects them to live like it.

He also meant to comfort. The quotation from Isaiah gives the Galatians something to rejoice in. The church might seem small, young and made of outsiders, yet it is the answer to the promise of a barren woman suddenly surrounded by children.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records Paul's way of reading two women and two sons. It does not hand later readers a licence to find hidden meanings in every Old Testament story. What Paul does here rests on three things: the historical facts of Genesis, God's own ordering of the line through Isaac, and an inspired apostle's authority to tell the church what the story pictures. A modern reader should follow his conclusions, not assume the same apostolic freedom to invent new correspondences.

The command inside the quotation, 'Expel the slave woman and her son,' is not a prescription for treating any group of people. In Genesis, Sarah spoke it, and God told Abraham to listen. Paul applies it to the principle of law as the basis of inheritance, not to flesh-and-blood neighbours. Reading it as a mandate to cast out descendants of Hagar or Ishmael would turn a statement about two ways of relating to God into a charge against people. Genesis itself shows God hearing Hagar and keeping His word to protect her son, Genesis 21:17-20.

What does carry forward is the instruction to measure every religious claim by the shape of the promise. Any teaching that makes belonging depend on human achievement stands in Hagar's line, however respectable.

debates.question: Is Paul's 'allegory' a free reading, or a pattern grounded in the history?

views.label: A typological reading of real history
views.case: The verb Paul uses says the events are 'being allegorized,' but he opens by saying 'it is written' that Abraham had two sons, and he treats them as historical persons. What he adds is the correspondence between two kinds of birth and two covenants. Many interpreters, from the Reformers onward, therefore speak of typology rather than allegory: the history comes first and the pattern is drawn from within it.

views.label: A deliberate ad hoc argument against the opponents
views.case: Some hold that Paul takes his opponents' favourite chapter and reads it with their own method, turning it back against them. On this view he is not teaching a method to imitate, but beating them at their own game. The weight of the passage still rests on the main argument of chapters 3 and 4, not on the cleverness of the correspondences.

views.label: The ancient allegorizing tradition
views.case: Others see Paul using the allegorical habits found in the Greek and Jewish world of his day. Even so, the church fathers who followed him disagreed about how far to copy him, and Paul himself roots the reading in promise and flesh, not in word-play on names.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the conclusion rests on what Genesis says about promise and flesh, and not on a free search for hidden meanings. A cautious reader should follow Paul where he leads and not use his example to build fresh allegories of their own.

debates.question: Who are the children of the 'present Jerusalem'?

views.label: The Judaizing movement and those who trust law for standing
views.case: Paul's concern is the agitators and those following them. The present Jerusalem stands for a religion of law as the way of belonging, tied to Sinai and the temple state. Paul does not speak here of the ethnic people as such, but of a system and of those who put themselves under it, including Gentiles who accept it.

views.label: Unbelieving Israel as a whole
views.case: Some read the line more broadly, as Paul placing the Jewish nation outside the promise for the moment. Romans 9 to 11 will not allow that reading, since Paul insists there that God has not rejected His people, Romans 11:1, and that their story is not finished.

debates.bearing: Romans 11 guards against reading this passage as a verdict on Jewish people. Galatians 4 is about two ways of standing before God, and it warns anyone, of any background, who tries to stand on the wrong ground.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's first move is a play on one verb. In verse 21 he asks whether they 'do not understand what the law says,' but the verb is the ordinary word for hearing. The law is something to be heard, and Paul suggests that those who are so eager to stand under it have never really listened. The two quotations in verses 27 and 30 then repeat the appeal to what the Scripture says.

Verse 23 uses a perfect tense for the births. Ishmael and Isaac 'have been born,' and Paul sets the two births under two phrases: 'according to the flesh' and 'through the promise.' The preposition changes as well, kata for the standard of the birth, dia for the means. The flesh here is not sinfulness in the abstract but ordinary human ability, a son produced by Abraham's strength and Sarai's plan, as Genesis 16:2 shows. The promise, in contrast, depends on the word and power of God, which is why Paul's verb in verse 29 for Isaac's birth sets him 'according to the Spirit.'

In verse 24 Paul calls the story something that is 'being allegorized.' The Greek is a participle, and it is not a call to treat Genesis as a puzzle. It means that the story says one thing and also speaks of another. In verse 25 the verb translated 'corresponds to' is a military sort of word, from a root meaning to stand in the same line or rank. Paul therefore places Hagar, Sinai and the present Jerusalem together in one column, and in verse 26 the Jerusalem above in the other. The Greek order is vivid: the slave column on one side, the free on the other, like soldiers lined up in files.

Verse 27 quotes Isaiah 54:1 almost exactly as it stands in the Septuagint, and the barren woman is called 'barren,' the very word used of Sarah in Genesis 11:30 in the Greek Old Testament. That connection between Isaiah and Sarah is not forced; Isaiah himself had linked them in Isaiah 51:2. Verse 29 uses the imperfect tense, 'was persecuting,' so the picture is of a continuing harassment, not a single insult. The Hebrew of Genesis 21:9 has the participle of the verb that makes the name Isaac, 'laughing,' and the BSB renders it 'mocking.' Paul calls it persecution, reading the scene in light of what the agitators were now doing to the Galatians.

Verse 30 quotes Genesis 21:10 with an imperative from the Septuagint, 'cast out,' the verb that will later be used for casting out of the vineyard or of the synagogue. Paul says it is 'Scripture' that speaks, though the words were originally said by Sarah, because God had told Abraham to heed her, Genesis 21:12.

typology.type: Isaac as the child born through promise
typology.fulfillment: Isaac was born when Sarah's womb was dead and Abraham's body was as good as dead, Romans 4:19, and the birth came only because God had said it would. Paul reads every believer as being born in that way: 'Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise,' verse 28. Where Isaac's birth was one miracle in a family, new birth by the Spirit is repeated across the nations, John 3:5-8. The type falls short because Isaac was a physical descendant of Abraham, while the Galatians are Gentiles who belong by faith, Galatians 3:29.

typology.type: Sarah's barrenness and the barren woman of Isaiah 54
typology.fulfillment: Sarah was the woman who could not bear and then bore a nation. Isaiah turned her into a picture for a ruined Jerusalem, and Paul sees the picture fulfilled when the church fills with Gentile children. The correspondence reaches its height in Christ's death and resurrection, since the Servant of Isaiah 53 is followed immediately by the song of the barren woman in Isaiah 54, as the cross is followed by the harvest of children. The type is still open, because the full number of the redeemed is yet to gather, Revelation 7:9.

typology.type: The two mountains and two cities
typology.fulfillment: Sinai is where the covenant at the mountain was sealed with fear and distance, Exodus 19:12 and Hebrews 12:18-21. The writer to the Hebrews sets that mountain against Mount Zion, 'the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22, where believers come to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant. Galatians has the same contrast in compressed form. The type falls short at one point: Sinai was not evil. It was a gift that served its time, Galatians 3:24, and the problem arises only when it is used as a ladder to belonging.

typology.type: The expulsion of the slave woman and her son
typology.fulfillment: In Genesis the casting out of Hagar and Ishmael separated the line of the covenant from a household rivalry. Paul reads the same logic in the church: law as the ground of inheritance cannot live in the same house as promise. The correspondence is fulfilled in Christ, in whom the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile has been taken down, Ephesians 2:14, and in whom 'there is neither slave nor free,' Galatians 3:28. The type is a warning about a principle, not a pattern for treating people, and God's care for Hagar and Ishmael in Genesis 21:17-19 shows that.

study.christ:
Christ does not appear by name in these verses, but He stands behind every line. Paul has already said that the promise was made to Abraham and to his seed, 'meaning One, who is Christ,' Galatians 3:16. The children of promise in chapter 4 are children only because they are in the One to whom the promise was made. When Paul says that the Jerusalem above is free, he is describing the community that has been set free by the Son, as Jesus Himself said in John 8:36, 'if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.'

The passage also shows why the cross matters in the story of two mothers. The slavery of Hagar's line is the slavery of those who are under the law and under its curse, Galatians 3:10. Christ redeemed those under the law, Galatians 4:4-5, so that they might receive adoption as sons. In that redemption the two columns meet. He was 'born of a woman, born under the law,' stepping into the household of the slave in order to bring its members out. The one who was born by promise, in a unique sense, is Himself the Son who frees.

There is a further link in the way Paul quotes Isaiah 54:1. The song of the barren woman follows directly on Isaiah 53, the Servant who was pierced for our transgressions, Isaiah 53:5. The many children of chapter 54 come out of the suffering of chapter 53. Paul does not make that argument in this passage, but it is the shape of the gospel he preaches: the Son is cut off, and a family without number is the result. Isaac's birth was a miracle at the beginning of the story, and the resurrection of Jesus is the greater miracle at its centre, from which the whole free family now takes its life.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Isaac is not simply a figure of Christ in this passage, and Paul does not make him one. Isaac is the pattern of the believer, and Christ is the one through whom the believer receives the promise. To read Isaac as Christ here would blur Paul's own line.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who keeps His word against all the odds. Sarah's age made Isaac's birth impossible, and God's promise stood anyway. Paul calls this 'promise,' and the word carries with it the stability of a God who does not lie. His choice of Isaac was not an afterthought to make up for a failed plan; it was the plan from the start, spoken in Genesis 17:19 before Isaac was conceived.

God is also the God who opposes the schemes of human self-help, yet who does not abandon those caught up in them. Hagar was a servant used by her mistress, and she was twice met by God in the wilderness. In Genesis 16:13 she called Him 'the God who sees me,' and in Genesis 21:17 God heard the boy crying and answered. Paul's argument does not erase those mercies. It shows that the same God who protected Ishmael did not let the covenant line be redefined by Abraham's and Sarah's plan.

He is a God who gathers. The Jerusalem above is a mother whose children are countless, and the God of Isaiah 54 promises that her tent will have to be enlarged, Isaiah 54:2-3. That is the language of expansive generosity. Paul reads the scattered, unlikely churches of Galatia as the first fruits of a promise that stretches the borders of God's family.

He is also the God who gives the Spirit as the mark of belonging. Isaac is described as born 'according to the Spirit,' verse 29, and Paul has already said in 4:6 that God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts crying 'Abba, Father.' The doctrine of God here is therefore Trinitarian in shape: the Father who promises, the Son who redeems, and the Spirit who brings the children to birth and testifies to their sonship, Romans 8:15-16.

For worship, the passage invites the Galatians to rejoice, which is exactly what the quotation says: 'Rejoice, O barren woman.' Nothing in the argument is meant to leave them anxious. The right response to a God who keeps promises that impossible circumstances cannot stop is to praise, and the right response to the freedom He gives is to stay in it.

crossReferences.note: The origin of the Hagar line. Sarai proposes to build a family through her servant and Abram listens to her voice. The wording recalls Genesis 3:17, where Adam also listened to the voice of his wife, and it shows the birth of Ishmael as a human solution to a divine promise.

God names Isaac before he is conceived and says the covenant will be established with him. He also promises to bless Ishmael, so Paul's argument does not rest on God hating Ishmael but on God choosing the line through which the covenant would pass.

The source of Paul's quotation. Sarah demands that the slave woman and her son be sent away, and God tells Abraham to listen to her because through Isaac the offspring will be reckoned. The same chapter shows God providing for Hagar and her son afterward.

The song Paul quotes in verse 27. A barren and desolate woman is told to rejoice because her children will outnumber those of the married wife, and to enlarge her tent. Paul hears this as the promise to Zion fulfilled in the Gentile mission.

Isaiah connects Sarah to the promise of restoration. God called Abraham alone and multiplied him, and He will comfort Zion and make her wilderness like Eden. This text prepares Paul's link between Sarah's barrenness and the exiles' hope.

A parallel argument from the same story. Not all who descend from Abraham are his children, because the line is reckoned through Isaac, and the children of the promise are regarded as offspring. Paul makes the same point from another angle and without the allegory.

The writer sets Mount Sinai, with its fire and trembling, against Mount Zion and the heavenly Jerusalem, where believers come to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant. It is the same contrast of two mountains, expressed in the language of approach to God.

The earlier statement of what verse 28 repeats. All who are in Christ are sons of God through faith, and if they belong to Christ they are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise. The allegory serves the argument made here.

Abraham's faith in the promise despite his own body's deadness and Sarah's barrenness. This is the human side of what Paul calls birth 'through the promise'. Isaac's birth is the reward of faith in a God who gives life to the dead.

Just before the allegory, Paul says God sent His Son to redeem those under the law so that they might receive adoption, and sent the Spirit of His Son into their hearts. The slavery-to-sonship movement of those verses is what the allegory then dramatises with two women.

study.oneStory:
The question that sits behind Galatians 4 was asked in the garden: whose word will the human family trust? In Genesis 3 the woman and then the man listened to a voice that offered a shortcut. In Genesis 16 Abram listened to the voice of his wife and a human plan was born alongside a divine promise. The contest between plan and promise runs the length of the Old Testament, from the barren wombs of the patriarchs to the exile in Babylon, and the question each time is whether God will do what He said without our help.

God answers by narrowing and then widening. The line narrows to Isaac, then to Jacob, then to Judah and David, and at last to one Man. But the promise to Abraham was always that all nations would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and Isaiah 54 imagines the barren woman breaking out in song as her tent is stretched to hold them. Paul says that this is what has begun to happen among the Galatians. The line that narrowed to Christ opens again in Him, and the children of promise come from every nation.

The two mountains also sit within the larger story. Sinai gave Israel the law as a guardian until the promised seed came, Galatians 3:19 and 3:24, and the temple and the earthly city were shadows of a greater dwelling of God with His people. Hebrews says believers have already come to that city, and Revelation shows it descending, 'prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2. The mother Paul calls 'the Jerusalem above' becomes the bride the Bible ends with.

In the new creation the question of Genesis 21 is finally settled. There is no rivalry in the house, no slave and no master, no one mocking and no one cast out. The inheritance that Isaac's line was promised is shared by all who are in Christ, Galatians 3:29, and the city has gates that are never shut, Revelation 21:25. The barren one who sat alone in exile is the city full of children, and God Himself dwells with them, Revelation 21:3.

sermon.title: Sons of Freedom (Galatians 4:21 to 31)
sermon.why: Begg unpacks the illustration of Hagar and Sarah as two covenants, showing that believers are children of promise born by the Spirit, citizens of the free Jerusalem above, and must not return to the slavery of the law.

quiz.q: What do Hagar and Sarah represent in Paul's illustration?

options.text: Two covenants, one of slavery under law and one of freedom by promise.
options.note: Verse 24 states the women represent two covenants.

options.text: Two rival nations at war with each other.
options.note: They picture covenants, not merely warring nations.

options.text: Two equally good ways to reach God.
options.note: One leads to slavery, the other to freedom; they are not equal.

options.text: Two stages every believer must pass through.
options.note: They are contrasting covenants, not sequential stages.

quiz.q: How was Isaac, the son of the free woman, born?

options.text: Through God's promise, not according to the flesh.
options.note: Verse 23 contrasts promise with flesh.

options.text: By ordinary human planning like Ishmael.
options.note: Ishmael was born according to the flesh; Isaac through promise.

options.text: By Abraham's obedience to the law.
options.note: Isaac was born by promise, long before the law was given.

options.text: By Sarah's own strength and youth.
options.note: Sarah was barren; Isaac came by God's promise and power.

quiz.q: To which mother do believers belong?

options.text: To the free woman and the Jerusalem above.
options.note: Verses 26 and 31 place believers among the free.

options.text: To Hagar and the present Jerusalem in slavery.
options.note: That is the covenant of slavery believers do not belong to.

options.text: To both mothers equally.
options.note: Paul says clearly we are children of the free woman, not the slave.

options.text: To neither; they have no mother in the story.
options.note: Believers are children of the free woman, the heavenly Jerusalem.

quiz.q: What does the quotation from Isaiah celebrate?

options.text: The once barren woman rejoicing over a countless family.
options.note: Verse 27 quotes Isaiah 54:1 about the desolate becoming fruitful.

options.text: The destruction of Jerusalem.
options.note: The song is about joyful fruitfulness, not destruction.

options.text: The triumph of the slave woman.
options.note: It celebrates the free and formerly barren woman, Sarah's line.

options.text: The end of all promises.
options.note: It celebrates the fulfillment of promise, a countless family.

quiz.q: What does Scripture command regarding the slave woman?

options.text: Expel the slave woman, for her son will not share the inheritance with the free son.
options.note: Verse 30 quotes Genesis 21:10 to exclude the way of slavery.

options.text: Keep both sons as equal heirs.
options.note: Scripture says the slave woman's son will not share the inheritance.

options.text: Give the inheritance to the slave woman's son.
options.note: The inheritance belongs to the free woman's son.

options.text: Ignore the whole matter of inheritance.
options.note: The inheritance is precisely the point; it goes to the free.

questions: Believers are children of promise, born by the Spirit and not by human effort. How does knowing your new life is God's gift, not your achievement, free you from striving?
Paul says the children of the flesh persecute the children of the Spirit. Have you experienced pressure or ridicule for resting in grace rather than performance?
The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. How does belonging to a heavenly city shape the way you hold the pressures of this present life?
Scripture calls the Galatians to refuse the way of slavery. What subtle forms of religious slavery do you need to send away?
Isaiah's barren woman rejoices over a countless family. How does the surprising fruitfulness of grace encourage you when your own efforts feel barren?

translationNotes.note: Illustrations renders a form of allegoreo; Paul draws out the God given pattern in the real history of Hagar and Sarah, not a denial that they lived.
Hagar corresponds to the present Jerusalem in slavery; the point is the covenant of law, not a comment on the geography alone.
The BSB footnote notes some manuscripts read we rather than you; either way believers are counted, like Isaac, as children of promise.
